characters: Nhyira: a gentle, observant eight-year-old Ghanaian girl in Primary 3 near Aburi, wearing a yellow-and-green school uniform, two neat Afro puffs with yellow ribbons, and holding a nature tally sheet.
Kojo: Nhyira’s eight-year-old classmate and nature-club partner, wearing a matching yellow-and-green school shirt and khaki shorts, holding a pencil.
Madam Serwaa: their Primary 3 teacher and nature-club leader, wearing a leafy-green dress and carrying a magnifying glass.
The Chipped-Wing Swallowtail: a black-and-yellow citrus swallowtail butterfly (Papilio demodocus) with a tiny v-shaped notch on its left hindwing.

narrationPlan.voice: Gentle, wonder-filled Ghanaian English storyteller for Primary 2–4.
narrationPlan.pace: Unhurried developing-reader pace (~110 words per minute).
notes: Pronounce Nhyira as NYEE-rah and Serwaa as sehr-WAAH.

culturalNotes: Encourages gentle scientific observation of Ghana’s rich biodiversity without harming insects.
reviewQuestions: Is the distinction between local butterfly navigation and continental migration clear and age-appropriate?
Does the observation activity enforce strict no-touch safety around insects?

pages.brief: Sunlit Ghanaian school garden with misty green Aburi hills in the background: Nhyira (8, yellow-and-green uniform, two Afro puffs with yellow ribbons, clipboard), Kojo (8, yellow-and-green uniform) and Madam Serwaa (green dress) observing colourful flowers.
pages.narration: Warm, gentle opening setting the safe and respectful observation rule.

pages.brief: Macro nature view: a black-and-yellow citrus swallowtail butterfly with a distinct tiny V-notch on its left hindwing perched on an orange lantana flower, uncoiling its spiral proboscis while Nhyira watches from a respectful distance.
pages.narration: Slow, wondering tone describing the notched wing and the uncoiling proboscis.

pages.brief: Morning sunlight in the school garden: Nhyira and Kojo looking in amazement as the exact same black-and-yellow butterfly with the tiny left-wing notch lands on the orange lantana bush.
pages.narration: Let Nhyira’s excitement and curiosity shine through.

pages.brief: Garden bench scene: Madam Serwaa holding up a large visual nature card showing a flower under human sight on one side and glowing purple-blue petal guide lines on the other side, while Nhyira and Kojo lean in curiously (no text on card).
pages.narration: Clear, vivid analogy comparing ultraviolet petal guides to runway lights.

pages.brief: Close-up of the black-and-yellow swallowtail resting on a glossy green citrus leaf, its two club-tipped antennae raised and its six legs touching the leaf surface.
pages.narration: Playful amazement on "smells with its antennae" and "taste sensors on its feet".

pages.brief: Close view of golden pollen grains on a butterfly visiting a red hibiscus flower, with Nhyira, Kojo and Madam Serwaa observing from the garden path.
pages.narration: Emphasise the scientific distinction that not all butterfly species migrate long distances.

pages.brief: Wide sunlit garden scene showing rays of morning sun above mango trees, flowering shrubs and the swallowtail gliding along the hedge path while Nhyira traces its path in the air with her finger.
pages.narration: Clear, accurate explanation of local habitat navigation using the Sun, scents and landmarks.

pages.brief: Nhyira and Kojo standing quietly by the flower bed holding a clipboard with tally marks (no readable words), watching yellow, white and black-and-yellow butterflies around the flowers.
pages.narration: Count the tally clearly: 6 yellow plus 4 swallowtails plus 5 white equals 15 visits.

pages.brief: Warm sunny finale in the school garden: Nhyira and Kojo watering potted hibiscus and lime seedlings with small watering cans while Madam Serwaa smiles and the swallowtail butterfly glides above.
pages.narration: Gentle, inspiring ending inviting young readers to observe and protect nature.

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 2–4 biodiversity, pollination and insect-navigation story set in a school garden near Aburi. Learners discover how butterflies use compound eyes (including ultraviolet vision), antennae and foot taste receptors, distinguish local habitat navigation from long-distance migration, and separate established biology from open neuroscience questions.
learningGoals: Describe how a butterfly uses its compound eyes, antennae, proboscis and feet to find and feed on flowers.
Explain how butterflies pollinate flowers while sipping nectar.
Explain that not all butterfly species migrate long distances; many Ghanaian butterflies navigate locally using sun position, scents and landmarks.
Distinguish what biologists already know about insect senses from what scientists are still discovering about tiny insect brains.

beforeReading: Ask learners: "Have you ever seen a butterfly visit a flower? How do you think it knows which flower has sweet nectar?"
Remind learners of the golden rule: we never catch, pinch or touch butterflies’ wings because the tiny scales rub off.
whileReading: Pause at page 5 and ask learners to point to their own noses and tongues, then compare where a butterfly smells (antennae) and tastes (feet).
Pause at page 7 to emphasise why scientists do not assume every butterfly acts like one famous species in another country.
afterReading: Take the class outdoors for a 10-minute silent Pollinator Tally Walk around flowering bushes on the school compound.
discussion: How could Nhyira be sure it was the exact same swallowtail butterfly on the second morning?
Why do flowers have bright colours, ultraviolet markings and sweet scents?
What is one question about butterfly brains that scientists are still investigating?
reflection: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? How could your class create a small "Pollinator Corner" at school or home using local flowering plants?

mathsExtension.task: Nhyira and Kojo counted 6 yellow grass butterflies, 4 black-and-yellow swallowtails and 5 white butterflies in 15 minutes. How many butterflies did they count altogether, and how many more yellow grass butterflies than swallowtails did they see?
mathsExtension.answer: Total = 6 + 4 + 5 = 15 butterflies. Difference = 6 − 4 = 2 more yellow grass butterflies than swallowtails.

support: Act out the four butterfly parts with hand gestures: unrolling proboscis (curled finger), antennae (two fingers above head), compound eyes (hands around eyes) and tasting feet (tapping toes).
stretch: Draw a simple bar chart comparing the 3 butterfly groups tallied on Page 8 (6 yellow, 4 swallowtail, 5 white).

culturalNotes: Aburi in the Akuapem South Municipality (Eastern Region) is home to the historic Aburi Botanical Gardens, famous for its rich plant and butterfly diversity.
localiseThis: Observe whatever pollinators visit flowers around your school, butterflies, honeybees, carpenter bees or sunbirds.

whatWeKnow: Butterflies see colour and ultraviolet light patterns with their compound eyes, detect airborne odours with their antennae, taste host-plant chemicals with receptors on their feet (tarsi), and sip liquid through a coiled proboscis.

Ghana has over 900 recorded butterfly species; unlike the North American monarch’s multi-generational continental migration, most Ghanaian species navigate locally or shift seasonally within West African habitats.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Neurobiologists are still investigating the exact neural circuits in the insect central complex that combine sun-compass cues, visual landmarks and odour plumes into spatial memory.

investigation.title: 10-Minute Quiet Pollinator Tally in the Schoolyard
materials: A notebook or sheet of paper ruled into 3 columns (Butterfly / Bee / Other Insect)
A flowering bush or garden patch on the school compound
steps: Stand two steps back from a sunny flowering bush so you do not cast a shadow over the flowers or disturb visiting insects.
For 10 minutes, stay quiet and make one tally mark each time a butterfly, bee or other insect lands on a flower.
Add up the tally marks in each column and compare which flower colour received the most visits.
investigation.whatToNotice: Staying still and quiet lets pollinators behave naturally, and different insects often prefer different flower shapes and colours!
investigation.safetyNote: Never touch, swat at or trap bees, wasps or butterflies; learners with insect-sting allergies should observe from a safe paved walkway with the teacher.

factCheck.claim: Ghana has over 900 butterfly species, and citrus swallowtails (Papilio demodocus) are common across Ghanaian gardens and farms.
factCheck.explanation: Torben Larsen’s Butterflies of West Africa documents over 900 butterfly species in Ghana, with Papilio demodocus widespread wherever citrus and garden flowers grow.
factCheck.reference: Larsen, T. B. (2005). Butterflies of West Africa; Ghana Wildlife Society.

pronunciation.guidance: roughly "NYEE-rah" with a breathy start. The "nhy" onset has no English equivalent.
reviewerNotes: HIGH RISK: "nhy" onset; the respelling is only an approximation. Needs a native demonstration.
